profiles.name: Aleksandr Ivanovich Batura
profiles.query: "Aleksandr Ivanovich Batura" IWW prisoner portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context:
Aleksandr Ivanovich Batura was employed as a migration: immigrated to us year unknown.

An anarchist and member of the IWW, he was arrested in Steubenville, Ohio, and deported to Poland on September 10, 1924. 

Upon return to Soviet territory he openly criticized living conditions and declared that “only Commissars and not workers live well here.” For these remarks he was sentenced to the Solovetsky prison camp and subsequently to internal exile. In correspondence circa 1927 he wrote to comrades in the U.S. reporting: “The main thing is that I have no work and it is so hard to get anything. I have been actually starving here, moreover, I am sick.” International anarchist networks sent him aid between 1929 and 1931.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Neil Guiney
profiles.query: "Neil Guiney" IWW prisoner portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context: Neil Guiney was an Industrial Workers of the World organizer born in British Columbia who entered the United States in 1913. He was arrested in St. Maries, Idaho, during the 1917 logging strike and acquitted of criminal syndicalism. He later became secretary of the Lumber Workers' Industrial Union and opened its Portland office. In 1919 he was detained in immigration proceedings over IWW literature he distributed. The Ninth Circuit upheld denial of his habeas petition on December 1, 1919, in Guiney v. Bonham, 261 F. 582. The opinion corrected a government letter falsely describing his Idaho case as a conviction and imprisonment in the state penitentiary. The deportation order does not establish his departure date or destination.

profiles.name: Steve Bratich
profiles.query: "Steve Bratich" Woodlawn sedition portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context:
Steve Bratich was the fourth defendant in the Woodlawn (Aliquippa), Pennsylvania sedition case, a group of Communist organizers of the Jones & Laughlin steelworkers arrested in a red raid on Armistice Day, 11 November 1926. Tried under Pennsylvania's Flynn anti-sedition law alongside Pete Muselin, Milan Resetar and Tom Zima, he was convicted in 1927 and sentenced to two and a half years' hard labour at the Allegheny County Workhouse at Blawnox — a lesser term than the five years the other three received. (the surname also appears as Bradich)

He was discharged on appeal in 1928 and so, unlike his co-defendants, never served the sentence. Their own appeals failed: the Pennsylvania Superior Court and Supreme Court both upheld the convictions, the United States Supreme Court declined to review them in 1929, and Muselin, Resetar and Zima entered Blawnox on 26 November 1929. Resetar died there.

This record was previously two, one under each spelling, each holding about half the case: Bratich had the arrest date and the account of the raid, Bradich had the 1927 conviction and the discharge on appeal. They are merged here and both spellings kept.
profiles.finding: Completed identity-specific portrait search; no sufficiently identified usable image verified. Sources indexed by query group; unresolved research remains open.

profiles.name: Tom Connors
profiles.query: "Tom Connors" IWW prisoner portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context: Tom Connors was an IWW officer. Tom Connors served a prison sentence in San Quentin from June 2, 1925, to Februaiy 1927. Connors was secretary of the IWW General Defense Committee in California. During his criminal syndicalism trial in Maryville, a prospective juror obtained a copy of literature printed by the General Defense Committee. The state of California dropped the criminal syndicalism charge against Connors and tried him for "corruptly attempting to influence a juror." Connors went through three trials on this charge. The first trial resulted in a hung jury; the second resulted in a conviction that was reversed by an appellate court. At the third trial Connors was found guilty and sentenced to three years of imprisonment.
